claims.evidence: General fact; no retrieved text states it word for word.
NHS treatment page: usually advised to try psychological treatment before medication; CBT available on NHS.
Talking therapies available without GP referral; can self-refer to a local service. Eligibility varies by area (England, GP-registered).
NHS 111 option 2 for crisis mental health support, free; Samaritans 116 123 free, around the clock; 999 or A&E if in immediate danger.
Attribution to the NHS not found in retrieved text; the general point is plain fact.
claims.newSentence: Feeling anxious now and then is a normal part of life.

claims.evidence: NHS: GAD is a long-term condition; anxious most days about a wide range of situations. 'Hard to control' not stated verbatim in text returned.
claims.newSentence: Generalised anxiety disorder, or GAD, is a long-term condition in which a person feels anxious most days, about a wide range of situations rather than one event.

claims.evidence: Guideline text: symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in important areas of functioning.
Found: restless or worried, trouble concentrating or sleeping, dizziness, palpitations; guideline adds fatigue, irritability, muscle tension. Stomach problems and low mood not found.
claims.newSentence: Alongside worry, symptoms can include feeling restless, trouble concentrating or sleeping, tiredness, irritability, muscle tension, dizziness and heart palpitations (a pounding or fluttering heartbeat).

claims.evidence: Mind: if unsure whether symptoms are anxiety or physical, a GP can look into possible causes.
NHS: exact cause isn't fully understood; several factors probably combine.
Inherited genes, past stressful or traumatic experiences, painful long-term health condition, history of drug or alcohol misuse.
NICE: comprehensive assessment not relying solely on number, severity and duration of symptoms, also distress and functional impairment. 'Current episode' and 'development over time' not found.
claims.newSentence: NICE advises a comprehensive assessment that looks at the number, severity and duration of symptoms, and also at the degree of distress and the effect on daily functioning.

claims.evidence: Distress and functional impairment supported; GP asking about past anxiety and mood history only partly seen (a NICE document lists past history of anxiety or mood disorders as a consideration, context unclear). Duplicates c12.
NICE: with a comorbid depressive or other anxiety disorder, treat the primary (more severe) disorder first.
GAD-2: two items on feelings of anxiety and ability to stop or control worry.
Usually advised to try psychological treatment before medication.
General definition of CBT.
CBT and applied relaxation available on the NHS is supported; 'one of the most effective treatments' not found in returned text.
claims.newSentence: CBT and applied relaxation are both talking therapies available on the NHS for GAD.

claims.evidence: NICE places self-help at step 2 (after step 1), as written or electronic materials worked through systematically over at least 6 weeks. 'First step' is not accurate.
claims.newSentence: NICE describes CBT-based self-help as a low-intensity step, with written or electronic materials worked through systematically over several weeks.

claims.evidence: If psychological treatment doesn't help, an SSRI should be offered; NHS: first medication is usually an SSRI antidepressant.
Stepped care supported (least intrusive, most effective intervention first); step 1 contents (identification, education, active monitoring) not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: NICE sets out treatment in steps, offering the least intrusive, most effective option first.

claims.evidence: Step 4: complex treatment-refractory GAD with very marked functional impairment or high risk of self-harm; highly specialist care.
Found: regular exercise, avoiding caffeine may reduce anxiety, healthy diet. Relaxation/breathing and the 'disrupt sleep' reason not found in returned text.
claims.newSentence: NHS self-help ideas include regular exercise, cutting back on caffeine, which may help reduce anxiety, and eating a healthy diet.

claims.evidence: NHS text found: drink alcohol in moderation and stop smoking. 'Advises against' alcohol, gambling and drugs not stated.
claims.newSentence: The NHS suggests drinking alcohol in moderation and stopping smoking as part of looking after physical health.

claims.evidence: There are lots of books and courses that can help you learn to cope with anxiety.
NHS: see a GP if struggling to cope and own efforts are not helping. Reword to match.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to speak to a GP if anxiety is hard to cope with and self-help is not enough.

claims.evidence: GP can discuss talking therapies, medication, referral; self-referral to NHS talking therapies possible.
Rethink and Mind pages found; Anxiety UK described as a user-led charity supporting people with anxiety (search summary only).
'Most people will not need emergency help' not stated in any retrieved text; 'treatable' is fair but reassurance claim is unsourced.
claims.newSentence: Anxiety is common and treatable, and there are several routes to help.

claims.evidence: Call 999 or go to A&E if in immediate danger. 'Physically harmed' not in returned text.
claims.newSentence: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E.

claims.evidence: NHS 111 option 2 for crisis mental health support, free, open around the clock (trust pages). 'On someone else's behalf' not confirmed in returned text.
claims.newSentence: For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which local NHS trusts describe as free and available at any time.

claims.evidence: Samaritans 116 123 free, around the clock.

notes: Counts reflect the original sentence status: those marked supported but edited were trimmed only for small extras. Several claims lean on search-summary text rather than verbatim page text; NICE CG113 pages returned date from about 2011 and a 2019 surveillance flagged a conflict on antidepressants with comorbid depression. c04/c27/c31 depend on England-only services and on local trust wording for 111 option 2. c13 duplicates c12 and is removed. Second-person 'If you or someone else' in c04/c30 is signposting, not a command, but could be softened. Phrases the NHS would not use: 'advises against ... gambling or drugs' (NHS says moderation/stop smoking).
